title: Where AI Fits in Content Work

production_notes: [VERSION] Tool capabilities described for Claude, ChatGPT, Canva, image generators and CapCut (AI features, automatic captions, free tiers) must be checked against the current products before recording. The script stays general on purpose.
Yuki and the Osaka bakery are fictional; stock footage must not show a real bakery name, logo or readable signs.
Scene 11 stock footage should show real bread being photographed, not AI-generated food, to match the point of the scene.

Hook.voiceover: It is Monday morning. Your list says three posts, one newsletter, two graphics and a short video, all by Friday. AI tools promise to help with all of it. But which tool helps with which job? And which jobs should stay with you?

Explain.voiceover: Hi, and welcome to AI for Content Creators and Marketers. In this first lesson, we look at where AI fits in the work you already do, and where it does not.

slide.title: Where AI Fits in Content Work
slide.body: AI for Content Creators and Marketers · Lesson 1 of 15

Explain.voiceover: Most content work follows the same six steps, for a large company or for your own small channel. Research, ideas, creation, editing, publishing, and finally measuring, where you look at results and decide what to change.

slide.title: Six steps of content work
slide.body: A horizontal flow of six numbered boxes, revealed one by one: 1 Research → 2 Ideas → 3 Creation → 4 Editing → 5 Publishing → 6 Measuring, with an arrow looping from Measuring back to Research.

Explain.voiceover: AI tools for content work fall into four main types. The first type is chat assistants, such as Claude or ChatGPT. They work with text. They are good at drafting, summarising, suggesting ideas and rewriting in a new tone. But they are weaker at facts. They can state wrong information in a very confident way.

slide.title: Type 1: Chat assistants
slide.body: Claude or ChatGPT · Good at: drafting, summarising, ideas, rewriting tone, tables and outlines · Weak at: facts (can be confidently wrong)

Explain.voiceover: The second type is design tools, such as Canva. They give you templates and layouts, and many now have AI features that suggest designs or remove backgrounds. They help you make consistent, branded graphics quickly.

slide.title: Type 2: Design tools
slide.body: Canva · Templates and layouts · AI features: suggest designs, remove backgrounds, create images · Good at: consistent branded graphics, fast

Explain.voiceover: The third type is image generators. They create new images from a written description, called a prompt. They are good for original illustrations and backgrounds, but they can struggle with text inside images, with hands and with exact details.

slide.title: Type 3: Image generators
slide.body: Left, green ticks: original illustrations · backgrounds. Right, amber warnings: text inside images · hands · exact details · licence terms vary.

Explain.voiceover: The fourth type is video editors, such as CapCut. They help you cut clips, add music and create automatic captions. They save time on the editing jobs you repeat every week.
Explain.stock_query: person editing short video on smartphone

Explain.voiceover: No single tool covers the whole workflow. And none of them knows your brand, your customers or your goals unless you tell it. AI can speed up the middle of the work a lot. But the first decision, what to say, and the last decision, whether it is ready to publish, stay with you.

slide.title: AI speeds up the middle
slide.body: The six-step flow again. Steps 2 to 5 glow teal with a small AI icon. Two large hand icons sit at the start (What to say?) and the end (Ready to publish?), labelled 'You decide'.

Explain.voiceover: Here is a simple way to picture it. Think of AI as a kitchen assistant. The assistant can chop vegetables and wash dishes very quickly. But the chef still chooses the recipe and tastes the dish before it goes to the customer. If the chef stops tasting, a mistake reaches the table. In content work, you are the chef.
Explain.stock_query: chef tasting sauce in restaurant kitchen
Explain.on_screen_text: In content work, you are the chef

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's look at an example. Yuki runs the social media channels for a small bakery in Osaka, Japan. She maps her weekly workflow, step by step.

For research, a chat assistant can group customer comments into themes. For ideas, it can suggest twenty post ideas from those themes. For creation, it can draft captions, and a design tool can help with graphics. For editing, it can suggest shorter versions. Scheduling features in her social apps can help with publishing. And for measuring, a chat assistant can summarise a small table of results.

slide.title: Yuki's workflow map
slide.body: Table, rows revealed one by one. Research → chat assistant: group comments into themes. Ideas → chat assistant: 20 ideas. Creation → chat assistant for captions; design tool for graphics. Editing → chat assistant: shorter versions. Publishing → scheduling features. Measuring → chat assistant: summarise results.

Demonstrate.voiceover: But Yuki decides that one step stays fully human: the photos of the bread. Her customers follow the bakery because the photos are real. An AI loaf might look attractive, but it is not the bread they can buy. She also decides that she will read and approve every caption before it is posted.

Many beginners think AI is most useful for creation. They ask it to write a post, and they publish the result. In practice, AI often helps most with the slow, repeated parts around creation: grouping research, listing ideas, making variations and summarising results.
The opposite mistake is using AI for the step where your own knowledge matters most, such as your opinion, or your real product photos. So decide which steps need you before you choose a tool.

slide.title: Decide first
slide.body: Large quote: "Decide which steps need you before you choose a tool."

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, content work usually follows six steps: research, ideas, creation, editing, publishing and measuring. Second, the four main AI tool types are chat assistants, design tools, image generators and video editors, and each is good at different jobs. Third, AI can speed up many steps, but you decide what to say and whether it is ready to publish.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Six steps: research, ideas, creation, editing, publishing, measuring. 2. Four tool types: chat assistants, design tools, image generators, video editors. 3. AI speeds up the work; you decide what to say and when it is ready.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will map your own content workflow in six steps. You will write which type of AI tool could help at each step, and circle the one step you want to keep fully human. It takes about fifteen minutes. In the next lesson, Teaching AI Your Brand Voice, we will make AI sound like you. See you there.
